issues.issue: Marketing and advance sales must begin "promptly after the Effective Date" and be reported "in such detail as MTC may reasonably request," neither of which is measurable. What constitutes compliance before any network exists is undefined.

A Party is "deemed to have accepted" test results unless it challenges within five business days, yet MTC need give the seven-day notice only "when doing so will not adversely impact the construction schedule." Whether deemed acceptance operates where no notice was given is not answered.

Network Operator must perform additional services on MTC's demand while the Parties "shall negotiate an amendment hereto that affords commercially reasonable terms" — an agreement to agree on the price of work already required. The compensation term is unenforceably open.

The duty to assist with "all information, material, documentation, and reports that may be reasonably required or requested by MTC" is open-ended and unpriced. Its outer limit against the cost allocation in Section 4.9.1 is not drawn.

The Ramp-Up Plan requires "approval by MTC, EOPSS and ITD," making Network Operator's performance depend on the consent of entities that are not Parties and on whom Section 12.11 confers no rights. What happens if EOPSS or ITD withholds approval is unaddressed.

This passage is cast as what "the Parties intend" and what ITD and EOPSS "will be responsible for," rather than as an obligation of either Party, leaving it unclear whether it is operative at all. The demarcation-point allocation on which it turns is itself left to the Fiber Management Plan.

Segment-by-segment responsibilities commence on acceptance testing, whereas Section 4.2.1 makes MTC solely responsible until the Commencement Date and Section 4.9.6 keys the operator's capital payments to the Commencement Date. When the operator's duties and payments actually start is not consistently stated.

The disclaimer refers to "the Contract Price earned by Design-Build Contractor," a capitalized term defined nowhere in this Agreement and drawn from a contract to which Network Operator is not a party. Its scope cannot be fixed from this instrument.

Network Operator takes over the Attachment Database only "beginning on the Commencement Date," yet Section 4.1.2 lists maintaining records in the Attachment Database among its general responsibilities without that limitation. The two provisions give different start dates for the same duty.

Network Operator must "develop" and submit "all Network Policies," but Section 2.44 defines Network Policies to include MTC's own Open Access Policy, FCC policies and a federal highway policy that the operator cannot author. The obligation cannot be squared with the defined term it uses.

The Fiber Management Plan draft is due "within six (6) months after execution of this Agreement," while Section 4.1.10.4 sets the same deliverable at six months "of the Effective Date." Execution and the Effective Date need not coincide, so the two deadlines can differ.

The section states only conditions on which MTC "will not approve" the plan, and criteria such as "excessive stranded segments of fiber" and consistency with "MBI's legislatively stated mission" have no defined content. Nothing obliges MTC to approve a conforming plan, leaving Section 4.5.2 without a completion mechanism.

The carve-out "except as otherwise expressly provided in this Section" does not say whether "this Section" means 4.5.4 alone or all of 4.5, which matters because Section 4.5.5 does give the operator ownership of its own extensions. The scope of the no-ownership rule is ambiguous.

Network Operator Network Extensions are declared "the sole property of the Network Operator," while Section 2.39 provides that an extension "shall become part of the MTC Network" unless the operator establishes otherwise to MTC's reasonable satisfaction. Ownership of the same facility is addressed by two rules that pull in opposite directions.

The Network Operator must engage "one or more qualified contractors" with no standard of qualification stated and no allocation of who bears the cost of the Interconnection work. Both are left to be supplied from outside the text.

Wholesale Customer-funded extensions are "the sole property of such Wholesale Customer or its designee," yet Section 2.39 makes any fiber optic cable extension part of the MTC Network unless the Network Operator proves otherwise. Nothing reconciles customer ownership with that default.

MTC "shall own any MBI Network Extension, regardless of the source of its funding," while Section 2.36 defines an MBI Network Extension as one "funded in whole or in part by MTC." The ownership rule and the definition describe different sets of facilities.

Network Operator "is required to periodically update or upgrade" the network to maintain carrier-grade quality, yet the same section funds all such work solely from the CAPEX Upgrade and Update Fund and caps even MTC-directed expenditures at the Fund's available balance. Whether the upgrade duty survives an exhausted Fund is unresolved.

Tasks "whether or not specifically described in this Agreement" are "deemed to be implied by and included within the scope of the Services" if required for their proper performance, which sets an unbounded catch-all against the detailed enumeration of duties in Article 4. What falls inside the Services is decided by a standard the clause does not supply.

Rates must not exceed "the Price Caps in Exhibit F," but the Agreement's exhibit list makes Exhibit D the Price Caps and Exhibit F the EOPSS/ITD Master Services Agreement, and the proviso then measures government rates against 85% of the Price Schedule rather than the caps. The rate ceiling actually applicable to MassDOT, EOPSS and ITD is indeterminate.

Third Party Service Provider contracts are assigned to MTC with effect "upon termination of this Agreement," while Section 8.5.1 provides that on expiration or termination such third party agreements are transferred only "on mutually acceptable terms and conditions" and at MTC's request. The automatic assignment and the negotiated transfer cannot both govern.

The price is fixed "at a the price of $60/mile/strand/month" but is simultaneously said to be the fee "pursuant to the Pricing Schedule, as the same may be adjusted from time to time" — and no "Pricing Schedule" is defined (Section 2.53 defines "Price Schedule"). Whether $60 is a fixed price or a floating schedule rate is unclear.

A fully conforming lease request must still be presented "to MTC for approval of the lease," with no standard governing MTC's decision, which sits awkwardly with the Open Access and non-discrimination policies incorporated by Section 2.44. Whether MTC may refuse a compliant request is unaddressed.

The Parties merely "will develop guidelines" for non-standard leases, with an "expectation" of accommodation and "favorable consideration" — precatory language creating no ascertainable obligation. Whether a refusal breaches this section cannot be determined from its terms.

Where the leased dark fiber is on a Network Operator Network Extension "contiguous with the dark fiber on the MTC Network," the operator contracts in its own name, but Section 4.7.4.5 requires a 50/50 split of payments for dark fiber on the MTC Network. A single contiguous lease straddling both is not allocated between the sections.

Only payments received "during the Term of this Agreement" are split 50/50, although an IRU is by nature a long-term instrument whose payments may fall due after the Term ends. Who takes post-Term IRU payments is not stated.

The Price Schedule must be consistent with "the Price Caps as set forth in Exhibit F, as amended from time to time pursuant to ARTICLE 6," but Article 6 gives the IPT only a recommending function and Section 6.2 requires a negotiated amendment for material pricing changes. How Price Caps are actually amended is left unclear.

This allows "the Price Schedules, including the Price Caps" to be updated annually with MTC's approval, whereas Section 12.1 permits modifications of the Agreement (of which the Price Caps exhibit is part) only "by a written document signed by both Parties." Whether an approved annual update amends the Agreement is unresolved.

The prohibition "Network Operator shall not provide Retail Services" is empty as drafted, because Section 2.57 defines Retail Service as "services provided by a Third Party Service Provider," a category that by Section 2.64 excludes the Network Operator. The prohibition and the definition cannot both be given effect.

The obligation to pay "all ongoing costs of operating the MTC Network ... and all costs of compliance with the terms of this Agreement" is followed by a long enumeration and then the catch-all "all other operating and monitoring expenses contemplated by this Agreement," against carve-outs for design and construction funding. Which side of that line a given cost falls on — and how far the funding duty extends — is contestable.

Exhibit I agreements are furnished "for informational purposes only," while Section 4.9.2.3 imposes administration responsibilities as to future agreements of essentially the same kind. Whether an Exhibit I agreement can later become one the operator must administer is not addressed.

The operator will have "the responsibilities described in this Agreement" with respect to Exhibit J agreements "when executed," without identifying which responsibilities or fixing the terms of agreements still in draft. The obligation assumed is unascertainable from the text.

This binds Network Operator to responsibilities under agreements MTC has not yet made, described only as ones "aimed at maintaining or enhancing the extent, structure, functioning and viability of the MTC Network" and "including but not limited to" property access agreements. The general words have no boundary against the specific examples given.

The estimate is made "a precondition to exercising the right to object set forth in Section 4.9.2.5," but Section 4.9.2.5 confers no right to object — it grants only a credit against revenue sharing. The precondition refers to a right that does not exist in the cited section.

The credit is for costs incurred "as a result of MTC's agreeing to the contractual term objected to," yet Section 4.9.2.4 requires only a written estimate and identification of differing terms and creates no objection procedure. Whether an objection was ever made, and what one is, cannot be determined between the two sections.

"This Subsection" is undefined — it may mean 4.9.2.6, 4.9.2.5, or the whole of 4.9.2 — so the reach of the mandatory dispute resolution referral is unclear. Nothing else in the section identifies the intended unit.

The operator acts as MTC's agent but expressly lacks authority to terminate, modify or waive anything under the third party agreements, while Section 4.1.9 makes it "administratively responsible for ensuring compliance with all of the requirements of such agreements." Responsibility without corresponding authority is a tension the Agreement does not resolve.

Payments are reduced "in proportion to the average shortfall (from 90%) in the percentage of CAIs that have been connected as of the end of each week during that period," a formula that does not say whether the reduction is proportional to the shortfall or to the connected percentage. The arithmetic of the relief cannot be performed with confidence.

MTC "represents and agrees" it will take commercially reasonable steps to have the network designed and built so the operator can meet the Agreement's parameters, while Section 4.2.1 makes MTC "solely responsible" for design decisions and leaves the operator only a right to comment. Where a design shortfall defeats SLA performance, which section governs is open.

This requires an "initial plan" whose only content requirement is a narrative, while Section 4.1.10.1 calls the same deliverable a capitalized "Initial Plan." The document's required contents and status as a defined deliverable are inconsistent between the two sections.

This is the provision that actually requires the Annual Plan, yet Section 2.4 defines "Annual Plan" as the plan submitted "pursuant to Section 4.9.2," a different subsection dealing with third party agreements. The defined term and its operative source do not match.

The fee schedule runs by "Year 1" through "Year 10" without saying whether a Year is measured from the Effective Date or the Commencement Date, though the Term itself ends on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date and payments commence with the Effective Date. Which year's rate applies in any given quarter is therefore uncertain.

The Year 1 rate "shall be paid on the Effective Date" ratably for the partial quarter, which does not sit with the main rule in Section 4.9.4 that the fee is paid "in four (4) equal parts at the beginning of each calendar quarter." Whether the first payment is a whole quarter or a prorated stub is contestable.

The formula multiplies the Year 10 fee by "100 plus the increase in CPI ... stated as a percentage," but the worked example converts a 15-point rise (150 to 165) into a multiplier of 110%, which the stated formula does not produce. The text and its own illustration give different answers.

The section directs "a determination of CPI Escalation," a capitalized term that appears nowhere else and is defined nowhere in Article 2. What is being determined, and by what measure, is left to inference.

Revenue sharing is computed on "Network Revenue attributable to that fiscal year," while Section 2.45 defines Network Revenue as revenue "recognized" under IFRS during the Term. Attribution and recognition are not the same test, and the difference decides which year's band applies.

MTC may divert "amounts in the Fund [that] exceed the amounts reasonably required for the purposes of the Fund," without any method for determining that amount, even though Section 4.6.1 makes the same Fund the only source of the operator's mandatory upgrade obligations. The size of the surplus is left to assertion.

MTC may in "its sole discretion" apply the decommissioning fund to "any purpose consistent with MBI's legislatively stated mission," a mission the Agreement nowhere identifies, while the operator's 2% payments continue regardless. The limit on MTC's use of the money is unascertainable from the instrument.

The statements must reflect "all Network Operator's assets, liabilities, income expenses, not limited to those related to the MTC Network" — a garbled enumeration that leaves it unclear whether income and expenses are one item or two and how far beyond the MTC Network the disclosure reaches. The scope of the reporting duty turns on that broken phrase.

The officer must certify absolutely that "there has been no fraud or intentional or willful misconduct by any Person," without any knowledge qualifier and using a capitalized "Person" that Article 2 does not define. The certification is broader than any officer could truthfully give.

The restriction covers contracts "having a stated duration of more than two (2) years for which application of IFRS would call for recognition of revenue ... more than two (2) years after actual receipt," and it is not clear whether both conditions must be met or the second merely explains the first. Whether an ordinary three-year wholesale contract needs consent turns on that reading.

Maintenance must comply with specifications "contained or incorporated, or to be contained or incorporated, in MTC's agreement with its Design-Build Contractor" — a document the operator is not party to and whose future contents are unknown — and with "the standards for carrier class networks." The governing standard is not ascertainable from this Agreement.

"Appropriate Scheduled Maintenance" is measured by Network Operator's "then current preventative maintenance procedures, which shall meet or exceed standard industry practice," letting the obligor set its own standard. "Standard industry practice" is given no content.

On cancellation or delay the operator "will comply with the provisions of the previous sentence to reschedule any delayed activity," but the immediately previous sentence concerns MTC's right to be present, not coordination or rescheduling. The cross-reference points to the wrong sentence.

Emergency Unscheduled Maintenance and Non-Emergency Unscheduled Maintenance overlap, since an "event imminently likely to cause" failure under 4.11.4.1 is also a "potential service-affecting situation" under 4.11.4.2, and only the latter carries a reporting deadline. Which category governs a given event is not determinable.

"Workmanlike care" is a lower and different standard from the warranty in Section 5.1.8 that the Services will be performed "in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards." Which standard governs maintenance work is not stated.

The operator must "apply any proceeds of such claims to the repair or replacement of the damaged property," while Section 10.3.4 names MTC as loss payee on the property policies and MTC owns the network. Who controls and receives the proceeds is answered differently by the two provisions.

Rental loss proceeds count as Network Revenue only "net of legal fees or other extraordinary costs of recovery," whereas Section 2.45 requires Network Revenue to be calculated "on a gross basis, without deductions or allowances" and expressly includes rental loss proceeds. The two measures of the same receipt conflict.

The operator must respond "as quickly as possible" with an allowance for circumstances beyond its reasonable control, a standard that does not align with the fixed restoration intervals contemplated by the SLAs and the MassDOT Operating Agreement referenced in the same sentence. Which measure governs a late restoration is unclear.

The operator may subcontract "any of the maintenance services hereunder," which sits against Section 12.10's bar on assigning the Agreement "in whole or in part" without consent. Where wholesale subcontracting shades into a partial assignment is not addressed.

MTC may direct testing "no more frequently than every five (5) years," a limit that sits against Section 4.14.1's right of access "at all reasonable times" to verify "the integrity of the operational status of the MTC Network." Whether MTC may effectively compel testing more often through its audit right is unresolved.

"Full compliance with all Network Policies" is required, but Section 2.44 lets MTC add "any additional policies reasonably required by MTC" at any time, and breach of this section is a ground for termination under Section 8.1.1. The obligation's content can be enlarged unilaterally after signature.

Performance is measured against "the SLA the Parties are in the process of completing," a document that is not attached and whose Exhibit E is blank. The central performance standard of the Agreement is left to future agreement.

The Parties "will review and agree to commercially reasonable changes" to the performance standards, an agreement to agree with no fallback if they do not. What happens on disagreement is left to a good-faith duty and nothing more.

Performance is measured against KPIs "as the same may evolve and be supplemented and enhanced during the Term," without saying who may change them or by what process. The measure of compliance is a moving and unowned target.

On an audit finding of incorrect accounting the operator must "promptly make all remunerative payments to MTC" — a word that has no settled meaning in this context and appears to be an error for corrective or remedial payments. The provision also says nothing about amounts found owing to the operator.

The operator must make "any changes and take other actions which are necessary" to maintain legal and Network Policy compliance, at unlimited cost and with no materiality or cost threshold. The boundary against Section 4.9.1's cost allocation is undrawn.

The carve-out reads "unless expressly constructed otherwise," evidently an error for "construed," and the limited-license characterization must also accommodate the IRU leasehold the operator may acquire under Section 3.6. The words as written do not say what displaces the license characterization.

The operator must supply and pay for all resources "necessary or appropriate" for the Services, a disjunctive standard in which "appropriate" has no limit. Read with Section 4.7.1's implied-services clause, the cost exposure is unbounded.

"An adequate number of trained and qualified personnel" sets no headcount, qualification or staffing benchmark other than the NOC's 24x7 requirement elsewhere. Adequacy is left to be judged after the fact.

MTC gives only "reasonable access" here, while Section 4.16.1 states that "MTC authorizes Network Operator all access to its facilities and premises needed to support the Services." The two grants of access are of different scope.

The Massachusetts office "shall be the headquarters for the Network Operator" without saying whether that means headquarters for the MTC Network operations or the corporate headquarters of the entity itself. The obligation assumed is materially different on the two readings.

Background check policies must be "no less stringent than the then-current requirements of MassDOT, ITD and EOPSS," requirements set by non-parties that may change at any time and are not annexed. The standard of compliance is not fixed by the Agreement.
